selective.label: Augustine: when a wound heals, it does not move into someone else.
A wounded body is still there, but it is no longer healthy.
The wound heals. The body becomes healthy again.
A cracked jar is still clay, but it cannot hold water.
Imagine: I take my friend’s share to make myself more comfortable.
Augustine: a good thing can be wanted wrongly—for example, putting my comfort ahead of what I owe my friend.
Is a wound a separate evil thing added to the body?
“Behold, it was very good.” Genesis calls creation good; Augustine uses this as a starting belief, not a result of our wound example.
In Augustine’s example, the wound is lost health—not an extra evil thing.
Because he believes God made things good, Augustine describes evil as damage within them—not a separate evil kind of thing.
In our example, I put my comfort ahead of my friend’s fair share.
Augustine compares two losses: the body lacks health; my selfish choice lacks fairness. Being injured is not itself a guilty choice.
Augustine’s answer: the injury belongs to the body; it is not a separate evil thing.
Augustine: a good creation can be damaged, and people can choose wrongly.
Paul: “The good that I would I do not”—I fail to do what I want.
Augustine’s starting belief: Adam’s first disobedience affects his descendants, so they are born needing rescue from sin.
Augustine’s church baptizes babies for forgiveness, before they can choose wrongdoing.
Augustine: God helps us love the good, not just know the rule.
Pelagius, as Augustine reports him: God gives ability, teaching and Christ’s example.
Augustine asks: do God-given ability and teaching fully explain our willing and doing good?
Augustine: sin damages human nature; it does not turn people into a separate evil kind of being.
Given his belief about Adam, Augustine explains infant baptism as forgiveness of shared sin—not of a wrong the baby personally chose.
Augustine’s answer: God helps us love and choose what is good.
Augustine: people need God’s forgiveness and inward help, not replacement as evil creatures.
“A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit.” What does the tree stand for?
People’s bodies are injured, grow weak and die. How should that be explained?
The writer asks: why create beings you know will go wrong?
An opponent replies: watching someone walk does not make them walk.
In the opponent’s comparison, the person acts; the watcher does not force them.
Taking the good-tree saying as a rule about origins, the writer argues that this harmful world needs an evil source opposed to the good God.
A watcher did not make the walker; the writer argues that the analogy does not excuse a creator who knowingly made the creature.
Augustine says damaged good; Two Principles says an opposing evil source.
An objection asks: if philosophy already studies God, why also need revealed teaching?
Aquinas: God intends a life with him that reason alone cannot fully discover.
Augustine’s person still chooses; Aquinas’s person still reasons. God’s help need not replace either.
Aquinas asks: can philosophy also show the goal we should live towards?
Aquinas: studying God does not mean reason can discover everything we need.
Aquinas: if we cannot discover our goal, God must make it known.
Because we need to know our goal and reason cannot discover it all, Aquinas says revelation is needed alongside philosophy.
Aquinas: causing harm does not prove a thing has an evil nature.
If wrongdoing is a choice, why does Augustine baptize babies for forgiveness?
A person’s bad choice does not yet answer the question about their maker.
Aquinas: to direct our lives, we need to know what we are aiming for.
Aquinas’s example: fire can work well as fire and still harm water.
Aquinas reads the tree as a person’s will: how they want and choose.
Aquinas reads the tree as a will producing actions; Two Principles reads it as a source producing things. That difference changes the argument.
